title: Your first Express app
idea: A first Express project is one file, `src/server.js`, that creates the app, adds routes and listens. A `package.json` records what it needs.
points: `express()` returns the app; every `app.get`, `app.post` and `app.use` call adds to it.
`app.listen` opens a port and returns at once; its callback runs when ready.
Keep code in `src/`; `package.json` and `package-lock.json` stay in the root.
`"type": "module"` in `package.json` makes `.js` files ES modules, so `import` works.

hero.caption: `src/` is a convention, not a rule: Node runs whatever file you name.

code.title: The app
code.caption: Save it as `src/server.js`. This copy calls itself once, then closes so the script can exit.

walk.text: Step one: import Express and create the app.
Step two: add a route. The handler waits for `GET /`; nothing runs yet.
Step three: `listen` opens a port. `0` asks the system for any free one.
`err` is set when listening failed, for example with `EADDRINUSE`.
Call the app once, print the reply, then close the server.

code.caption: A `package.json` for this app, trimmed to what it uses.

walk.text: `npm install express` adds this entry. The `^` range is explained next.

pitfalls: Without `if (err) throw err`, a busy port looks like success: the callback still runs.
Never edit `node_modules`; delete it and run `npm install` to get a clean copy.
Edits to `server.js` apply only after you stop the process and run it again.

quiz.why: `listen` returns at once, so `started` prints first. The callback runs once the port is open. No request arrives, so the handler never runs.

takeaway: Registering a route does not run it; only a request does.

starters: Why does the book use `listen(0)` instead of a fixed port?
